newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan court defers Bhutto case against ouster.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan court defers Bhutto case against ouster.

text.p: A legal action by sacked Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto to have her government restored was deferred by the Supreme Court on Saturday.

The court said it would first consider petitions challenging the controversial Eighth Amendment, used by President Farooq Leghari to dismiss the National Assembly (lower house) and Bhutto's government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Leghari meanwhile filed a 202-page document with the Supreme Court on Saturday to justify his decision, citing alleged corruption and malpractices by Bhutto's government.
"We have decided to take up cases on the Eighth Amendment first as we want to first dispose of the controversy on it," Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah declared.
"We know that other cases are equally important including Benazir Bhutto's case," the official news agency APP quoted Shah, who was heading a seven-member bench, as saying.
Bhutto's lawyer Aitzaz Ahsan said he accepted the court's decision, but hoped it would not prejudice what he called the right of the ousted government to be restored before the polls.
Shah said the court was aware of the approaching elections on February 3 and promised to deal promptly with Bhutto's plea.
The court decided to amalgamate all petitions challenging the article, dating from the martial law era, used by Leghari to sack Bhutto and dissolve the National Assembly.
The Eighth Amendment was inserted into the constitution in 1985 by former military ruler General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq.
A lawyer for one of the petitioners, Mehmud Achakzai, a deputy in the defunct National Assembly, said the Eighth Amendment had removed the sovereignty of parliament.
He said it gave enormous discretionary powers to one person to dissolve the lower house and dismiss an elected government without being held accountable to the people or losing office.
Leghari, picked as Bhutto's presidential nominee after the 1993 election, said after taking office that he would never use his powers to dismiss an elected government.
Leghari, once a member of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, says he acted in the national interest. "It was a very painful decision, but the choice for me was very clear," he said.
In his new document, the president elaborated the nine reasons he had given at the time, accusing the former government of institutionalising corruption, nepotism and abuse of power.
He said the Bhutto government had defied Supreme Court orders, bugged telephones and allowed law and order to deteriorate and extra-judicial killings to take place.
Leghari argued that thousands of people had been appointed illegally and "the public exchequer was treated as though it were the personal kitty of the prime minister and her cohorts".
He cited the September 20 death of Bhutto's brother Murtaza in Karachi as further evidence of a government breakdown.
"When the prime minister's own brother is brutally murdered by the police, when the prime minister on the one hand speaks of a conspiracy and on the other engages in a cover-up;

"When the killers of the deceased are readily identifiable but not arrested for 30 long days; when those holding high office are directly implicated in the murder then certainly a situation has arisen where the government...is not being... carried on in accordance with the constitution," the paper said.
Bhutto has accused Leghari of being behind her brother's killing, a charge the president has dismissed as "ridiculous".
